title: 元朝秘史 §§1–6
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§1–6
workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§1–6, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇), applied consistently and not normalised to any later standard. Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol, and any reading convention would be a modern invention.
about: The opening of the Secret History — the oldest Mongolian literary work, written not long after Chinggis Qahan's death. Read it knowing what it is: the Mongolian original, in Mongolian script, is lost. What survives is a Ming-dynasty teaching edition made at the Hanlin Academy, in which the Mongolian was written out phonetically in Chinese characters, with a Chinese gloss over every word, so that interpreters could learn the language. So the characters on this page are Chinese, and mean nothing in Chinese: 成吉思 is not 'become-lucky-this', it is simply the sounds Či-ṅgi-s. The Mongol word is the line beneath, and it is a reconstruction — scholars differ over the vowels, and the Chinese script cannot show some distinctions at all. The glosses in square brackets are the Ming glossators' own, six hundred years old. Tap a word for both. The transcription also writes a small auxiliary character beside the main one for sounds Chinese has no character for — a little 舌 'tongue' for a trilled r, a small 中 for the back q and γ, and a small 勒 克 黑 惕 for a consonant closing a syllable. They are shown here at ordinary size. A few of the characters are rare enough that some devices have no font for them and will show an empty box.
draftNote: Pilot — the first Secret History text in Lectorium. The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting and is still being checked.

sentences.n: in-ü is the third-person genitive, 'his', and Middle Mongol puts it after the noun it belongs to. maral is the hind, the female red deer; like Börte Chino, Qo'ai Maral doubles as a name.

to cross over (water); imperfective converb -žü, 'crossing' [渡着]

sentences.n: -žü / -žu is the imperfective converb, the workhorse of Mongol narrative: it hangs an action onto the finite verb that follows — 'crossing … came'. You will meet it constantly, often five or six deep. The Ming gloss marks it with 着, Chinese's own nearest equivalent. Teṅgis is glossed 水名, 'name of a water' — an inland sea or great lake.

sentences.l: Batachiqan's son Tamacha, Tamacha's son Qorichar-Mergen, Qorichar-Mergen's son Aqujam-Boroqul, Aqujam-Boroqul's son Sali-Qachaqu, Sali-Qachaqu's son Yeke-Nidün, Yeke-Nidün's son Simsochi, Simsochi's son Qarchu,
sentences.i: Batachiqan's son was Tamacha; Tamacha's son, Qorichar-Mergen; Qorichar-Mergen's son, Aqujam-Boroqul; Aqujam-Boroqul's son, Sali-Qachaqu; Sali-Qachaqu's son, Yeke-Nidün; Yeke-Nidün's son, Simsochi; Simsochi's son, Qarchu.
sentences.n: The genealogy runs on one frame with no verb in it at all: possessor in the genitive, then köġün 'son', then the name. Middle Mongol needs no copula here and the Ming glossators supply none either. Watch the genitive change shape to suit the word before it — -jin after a vowel (Tamača-jin), -un/-ün after a consonant (Aγ̇užam-Boroγ̇ul-un), -(n)u/-(n)ü after -n. That is vowel harmony, the spine of the language; but note that the Chinese character 訥 writes both -nu and -nü, so which one is printed here is the editor's decision, not the manuscript's.

sentences.n: The whole line hangs off a single 'there was', everything before it built with the possessive -tü/-tu: wife-having, young-man-having, geldings-having. külüġüd is a plural, 'swift ones'; aγtastu is aγta 'gelding' + the plural -s + -tu. Bajan means 'rich' — Toroqoljin the Rich.

sentences.n: qojar 'two' follows the pair it counts and does the work English gives to 'both' — Mongol has no plural agreement to lean on. The epithets carry the characterisation in this text: soqor is 'one-eyed, blind', mergen 'the good shot, the wise one'.

sentences.l: Duwa-Soqor, in the middle of his forehead a single eye-having, over a land of three moves used to see.
sentences.i: Duwa-Soqor had a single eye in the middle of his forehead, and with it he could see a distance of three days' march.
sentences.n: neġürid is the plural of neġüri, one stage of a nomadic move — the distance a camp travels before pitching again — so 'three moves' measures ground, not time. qaraqu büleġe pairs an imperfective participle with 'was' to make a past habitual: not 'saw once' but 'could see, used to see'.

sentences.n: deġü-lüġe-beġen stacks three pieces into one word: deġü 'younger brother', -lüġe 'together with', -beġen the reflexive-possessive 'his own'. The Ming gloss unpacks it in exactly that order — 弟 一同 自的. The reflexive possessive marks something belonging to the sentence's own subject, a distinction English simply drops.

sentences.l: Duwa-Soqor, from the top of Burqan Qaldun looking, along the Tünggelig stream a band of people moving camp and coming down, their coming looking at and seeing, said:
sentences.i: Looking out from the top of Burqan Qaldun, Duwa-Soqor saw a band of people coming down along the Tünggelig stream with their camp on the move, and he said:
sentences.n: Six converbs in a row — qaražu, neġüžü, orožu, qaražu, üžežü, ügülerün — and still no finite verb. This is how Middle Mongol builds a long sentence: a chain of '-ing' forms hanging off one conclusion, which here does not arrive until the end of §6. aisuqu-ji is the imperfective participle 'coming' with the accusative -ji, so what he sees is 'the coming' of the people, not the people themselves.
